The Vendors Feature: Background & Vision

How it works, why it works that way, and an invitation to the people running similar efforts.

This page is for residents who take a deeper interest in how the vendor listings work — especially those who run, or help run, other vendor-recommendation efforts in Sun City. It explains what has been built, the reasoning behind the design choices, and where this could go with your help.

The problem being solved

Vendor recommendations are among the most requested and most valuable information residents share — and among the worst-preserved. In most places they live in scrolling feeds and group chats: a great recommendation posted in a group helps the people who happen to see it that week, then sinks. Six months later someone asks the same question and the answer is re-typed from memory, or lost. Search in these tools is weak, membership is closed, and nothing accumulates: the tenth recommendation for the same plumber carries no more weight than the first.

The most organized efforts go further — a dedicated volunteer collects submissions and periodically assembles them into a shared list posted back to the group. That work proves how much residents value a real directory, and it deserves credit. It also shows the limits of hand assembly: the result is a snapshot that ages between updates, it is only as browsable as a document in a group's files area, it reaches only that group's members, and the whole thing rests on one person's continuing labor.

The guide's vendor feature is an attempt to give those same community recommendations a durable, structured, searchable home — without losing what makes them trustworthy, which is that they come from neighbors, and without asking any one volunteer to assemble it by hand forever.

How it works today

The heart of it is a simple pipeline: recommend → review → publish.

  • Recommending. Any verified resident can submit a vendor they have personally used — name, category, contact details, and what the vendor did for them. Takes about a minute.
  • Review. Every submission is reviewed by an administrator before it appears: names and categories are normalized, and anything inappropriate is filtered. Nothing publishes automatically.
  • One listing per vendor. When several residents recommend the same vendor, the submissions merge into a single listing: recommendation counts add up (“Recommended by 3 residents”), contact details fill in from whichever submission had them, and comments combine. Repeat recommendations make a listing stronger, not noisier.
  • Browsing. The public vendors page shows every service category — plumbing to pet care to patios — with listings grouped, counted, and deep-linkable (e.g. /vendors/#plumbing). Featured placements — sponsored listings drawn from the same resident-recommended pool, and labeled as such — appear at the top of their category listings; the sponsors page explains the program.
  • Wider search. Inside any category, a resident can also run a web search of nearby providers (Google-powered). Those results are clearly labeled as not resident-recommended — useful where our own list is still thin, and every web-found vendor who works out is a candidate for a real recommendation.
  • Ask the Guide. Signed-in residents can simply ask the community chat (“can anyone recommend a plumber?”) and get resident recommendations alongside nearby options, with the same labeling.
  • Researched listings. Most listings were seeded by research rather than by a recommendation: each carries a one-line description, specialty tags, and — for medical practices — dated facts such as whether new patients are being accepted, Medicare acceptance, and the hospitals CMS records associate with the practice’s clinicians. The dots (below) show how well documented a researched listing is.
  • Research Briefs. A few listings now carry a full Research Brief — a sourced report checked against official records. The section below explains the idea; commissioning your own is coming.
  • Problems. Residents can report a bad experience privately. Reports go only to the administrators — nothing negative is ever published — and repeated concerns about a vendor over a period may result in administrative removal from the list.

Design decisions, and why

Several choices here are deliberate, and worth explaining to anyone who has wrestled with the same trade-offs:

  • Curated, not open-posting. Open forums self-moderate through volume; a directory can't. Review-before- publish keeps quality high, keeps spam and self-promotion out, and means every listing is accountable to a named (but unpublished) recommender.
  • Positive-or-absent — no published negatives. Publishing complaints about named local businesses invites disputes and legal exposure that a resident-run effort should not carry, and one-sided accounts presented as fact don't serve residents either. Instead, concerns are collected privately, patterns are watched, and the consequence is quiet removal. On a curated list, absence is the signal.
  • Verified residents, private identities. Recommending and reporting require resident sign-in — so every input is accountable — but recommender and reporter names are never published or shared. Listings show only counts.
  • Structured records, not threads. A recommendation captured as data (category, contacts, count) can be browsed, searched, merged, counted, and cited by the chat assistant. A recommendation captured as a chat message can only be scrolled past.
  • The web search knows its place. The wider Google search is bounded to our service categories (which keeps its costs controlled and predictable) and its results are always labeled as not resident-recommended. It supplements the community's knowledge; it never impersonates it.
  • No platform lock-in. The entire vendor database can be exported by an administrator to an ordinary spreadsheet at any time. If this effort ever ends or changes hands, the community's accumulated recommendations are a file, not a hostage.

What the dots mean

Some listings carry a dot indicator — ●●● Well documented, ●●○ Partially documented, or ●○○ Limited info. The dots show how much we could learn about the business from public records when the listing was researched — not a star rating, a quality score, or an endorsement of the vendor.

  • ●●● Well documented. Service in the Sun City area is reasonably confirmed, the business appears legitimate and active, and a meaningful positive public record was found — reviews with real history, credentials, licensing where it applies.
  • ●●○ Partially documented. The business appears legitimate and relevant, but a gap remains — for example, limited reviews, no explicit Sun City coverage confirmed, or licensing we could not verify.
  • ●○○ Limited info. We found the business but could not verify much about it. Check it out yourself — coverage, licensing, current operation — before hiring.

The dots appear only on listings no resident has yet reported using. Once residents report using a vendor, that count is shown instead — a neighbor's actual experience says more than our homework does. The level is set by an administrator from source evidence and never moves automatically because a vendor gets recommended, becomes resident-owned, or becomes a paid sponsor. As with any listing here, use your own judgment when hiring — the dots describe how much homework has been done, not a guarantee of the outcome.

How listings are ordered

Within a category, listings appear in this order:

  1. Featured listings first, clearly labeled as a paid sponsorship.
  2. Then vendors at least one resident has personally recommended.
  3. Then by how well documented the listing is — ●●●, then ●●○, then ●○○.
  4. Then by how many residents have recommended the vendor.
  5. Finally, alphabetically by name, as a tie-breaker.

This is presentation order, not a ranking of who is “best.” A listing placed first because it is a paid sponsor, or because more residents happen to have recommended it, is not necessarily the better fit for your particular job — read the listing, not just its position.

Research Briefs

A listing tells you a business exists and how to reach it. A Research Brief tells you what the public record actually says about it — and, just as important, what it doesn’t. Three finished briefs are live now (Harbor Point Dentistry, Novant Health New Riverside Primary Care, and Bluffton Electric), and residents can now commission new ones on supported categories.

What a brief contains

  • Identity and contact, checked against state business and licensing records — so the brief is about the exact business or practitioner, not a similarly named one.
  • Official records: state license status and public board actions, looked up directly and dated; for medical practices, each clinician’s license, board certification where a board publishes it, and the hospitals CMS records associate with them.
  • Services and terms, clearly attributed to the business when that is the only source.
  • What independent reviews do and don’t show — recurring themes only, never a verdict.
  • Questions to ask before hiring or scheduling, and a plain account of what the research could not establish.

The rules it follows

  • Evidence before fluency. Every material statement traces to a source that was actually retrieved, with the date. An unknown is labeled “not verified,” never filled in.
  • Uncertainty is part of the product. Gaps, conflicts between sources, and records that could not be reached are shown, not buried.
  • Absence is never a clean record. A public lookup that shows no board orders means exactly that and nothing more; complaints and nonpublic matters fall outside it.
  • No ranking, no score, no endorsement. A brief describes evidence quality, never business quality, and it never calls anyone the best.
  • Medical and dental briefs stop at the consultation door. They help you evaluate access, identity, licensure, coverage, and fit. They never judge clinical competence, whether treatment was appropriate, or which clinician is better.
  • Adverse information needs an official record and an exact match. Reviews, social posts, and copied directories are never the sole basis for a damaging claim; ambiguity means omission.

How commissioning will work

The model is commissioned, then communal. A resident asks for a brief on a listing that doesn’t have one; once the research is done and passes its checks — usually within a day or two, occasionally longer when an official record has to be rechecked — the brief becomes part of the shared directory, readable by every verified resident. Paying for a brief buys priority and a contribution to the community — not a favorable conclusion, and not private ownership of the result. If the business can’t be identified with confidence or the public evidence is too thin to be useful, no brief is published and the resident isn’t charged.

Research, resident recommendations, and sponsorship are kept visibly separate: a sponsor’s status never changes what a brief finds, a brief never counts as a recommendation, and neither affects the other’s labels. A business may commission a brief about itself only under the same rules, with that fact disclosed. Corrections are always free — anyone, including the business, can point to a specific statement and the source it should be checked against.

Briefs are produced by AI-assisted research checked against official records and reviewed before publication. During the pilot phase, credits are granted by site administrators on request. Visit the Research Briefs page for details on how to get started.

Where it stands

As of late August 2026 the directory holds more than 1,500 listings across 31 service categories — seeded from resident-shared lists and a category-by-category research pass, and growing through the recommendation form. The vendors page, the categories and specialty filters, the researched descriptions and dated medical facts, the recommendation and reporting forms, the web-search augmentation, the chat integration, and the first three Research Briefs are all live. Commissioning briefs is the next piece.

The vision — and an invitation

Sun City already has residents doing this work — notably the vendor-recommendation Facebook group and the TeamReach group. Those communities have something this system doesn't: active conversation, trust built over years, and a large accumulated body of recommendations. This system has what the feeds lack: permanence, structure, search, and a home that any resident can reach without joining anything.

Those are complementary strengths, not competing ones. The groups are where recommendations happen; this can be where they last. Some concrete forms collaboration could take, in increasing order of ambition:

  • Cross-linking. The groups point members at the vendors page as the durable reference; the guide points residents who want discussion toward the groups.
  • Importing the archive — where that's possible. Where an administrator already maintains an assembled list of their group's recommendations, that list could — with their blessing — be reviewed and folded into the structured directory, preserving years of community knowledge in one step. Where platform rules make exporting past posts impractical, the path is prospective instead: the group shares a link to the recommendation form and encourages members to submit there in addition to posting in the group — the conversation stays where it lives, and the recommendation also lands somewhere permanent.
  • Shared stewardship. Group administrators — some of whom already collect and assemble recommendations by hand — are exactly the right people to help review submissions, watch categories they know well, or shape policy. This system automates the assembly, publishing, merging, and counting; the human judgment stays, shared among more hands.
  • Consolidation, if and when it earns it. If this system proves itself the better home, groups could retire their parallel record-keeping in its favor — on their timeline, by their choice.

If you help run one of these efforts and any of this interests you — or you think parts of it are wrong — please reach out through the contact form. Skeptical feedback is as welcome as enthusiasm; you know failure modes of this work that I haven't hit yet.

The guide is an independent, resident-created project — not an official Community Association service. Vendor listings are a convenience, not an endorsement; residents should use their own judgment when hiring. See the about page for the full picture.
